newsitem.title: USA: CANTV offer seen as Venezuela test.
newsitem.headline: CANTV offer seen as Venezuela test.

text.p: The $1 billion global offering of Venezuelan telephone company CANTV's shares on Friday is as much a test of the South American country's economic reforms as of the company itself, analysts said.

They said the sale of most of the Venezuelan government's 49 percent stake on the New York Stock Exchange and other markets would be a good chance for portfolio managers to include a Venezulan share in their basket of Latin American stocks.

"It's being sold in terms of being a Venezuela story. They are not really marketing it in terms of, 'Here's CANTV and you should buy it,'" said Julie Dykstra, Venezuelan country analyst for Bear Stearns & Co.
Company officials have said they hope to raise between $900 million and $1 billion in the sale, one of the biggest international offerings out of Latin America this year.

Analysts predicted the offer would not draw the strong interest other Latin American telecommunications offerings have. However, it is something of a measure of confidence in modest economic reforms under President Rafael Caldera.

Following an agreement with the International Monetary Fund to carry out tight fiscal and monetary policies, the government has predicted inflation will fall to 30 percent next year from 100 percent in 1996.

However, Venezuela has postponed privatization of a number of banks despite a vow to sell more than a dozen big state companies. Underscoring the importance of the CANTV offer, Finance Minister Luis Raul Azocar will attend the launch in New York.

"You are kind of taking a negative bet on Venezuela if you don't own it, and that in itself will bring a lot of people into the deal," said Brian Barish, head of emerging market research at Lazard Freres.
Analysts said CANTV -- an acronym for Compania Anonima Nacional Telefonos de Venezuela -- faces other obstacles besides Venezuela's economic climate.
Its penetration rate of 11.5 lines per 100 people is in line with much of Latin America, and its telephone rates are well below the regional average.
It has not had a tariff adjustment in years despite government promises. The company aims to increase the number of lines from 2.1 million to three million by the end of the year 2000.
"The other issue is the quality of the deal, and I don't see it as a screaming deal at all," said Jose Linares, Latin American telecommunications analyst at Oppenheimer & Co.

Analysts said the offer probably would fall well short of the rate of six or seven orders for each share that recent Latin American telecommunications issues have seen. A total of 289.4 million Class D shares have been put up for sale.
A boost to demand came on Wednesday from GTE Corp. It said it would buy up to $200 million of the offering, thus increasing GTE's individual stake in the company to 26 percent from 20.4 percent.
More than 80 percent of the CANTV shares are to be sold as American Depositary Receipts (ADRs) listed on the New York Stock Exchange and in London. Each will represent seven Class D shares.
Shares were offered this week in Venezuela and orders there totaled $313 million, far above the official target of $200 million.

The initial public offering in New York is exepcted to be priced between $21.50 and $24.50 an ADR. Final pricing for CANTV will take place on Thursday, and trade starts on Friday under the symbol VNT.N.
Lead underwriters for the issue are SBC Warburg and Lehman Brothers.
